cases.label: emit-dtstart
cases.note: DTSTART is emitted as instance 1 even though 1997-09-02 is a Tuesday and not the 13th. This is JSCalendar's legislated behaviour and the reading the RFC's own Friday-the-13th example (which EXDATEs DTSTART away) presupposes.

cases.label: rule-only
cases.note: DTSTART is a seed only; the set contains rule matches at or after it. python-dateutil, rrule.js and most engines behave this way.

cases.label: reject
cases.note: Refuse the rule as undefined per the literal text of §3.8.5.3.

expectation.note: Three readings, one of which the RFC's own example depends on and another of which it declares undefined.

normative_evidence.quote: If the specified recurrence rule does not include the start date-time, then the recurrence instances ... are undefined.

normative_evidence.note: REJECTED, on the ground that 'the original example intentionally demonstrates the EXDATE feature by excluding the first occurrence' — which presupposes DTSTART *is* emitted. The RFC Editor thereby endorsed the emit reading inside an errata rejection note, which has no normative standing.

normative_evidence.quote: the start date-time ... is always the first occurrence in the expansion ... even if it would normally not match the rule

rationale: DTSTART's role is the deepest under-specification in RFC 5545. §3.8.5.3 says the case is undefined; the same section prints an example that only works if DTSTART is emitted; erratum 5920's rejection entrenches the contradiction; RFC 8984 fixes it in the opposite direction to the ecosystem. Manufacturing a single answer here would be dishonest.
title: DTSTART unsynchronised with the rule (the RFC calls this undefined)
